issues.legal_issue: Further enhancement of compensation for acquired land requires material supporting a market value above the value already determined by the reviewing court.
material_facts: Land was acquired for a public purpose, and the compensation was successively increased by the reference court and the High Court.
The claimants presented no material supporting a market value higher than the value fixed by the High Court.
issues.conclusion: The Court found no ground to interfere with the High Court’s valuation or to grant a further enhancement, and dismissed the special leave petitions.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 4(1), 11 and 18 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, compensation is determined by reference to the market value of the acquired land. The Court declined further enhancement because no material was shown to support a value above that determined by the High Court; no earlier cases were relied on for this ruling.

predicates.compensation_enhancement_case: The proceeding seeks an increase in compensation for acquired land.
predicates.prior_court_increased_market_value: A reviewing court has already increased the market value fixed for the acquired land.
predicates.no_material_supports_further_increase: The party seeking a further increase presents no material supporting a market value above the value already fixed.

issues.definition: When a compensation-enhancement proceeding follows an increase by a reviewing court and no material supports a further increase, further enhancement is denied.

issues.legal_issue: An election petition whose filing period expires while the High Court is closed for ordinary business may be filed on the first day the High Court reopens.
material_facts: The period for filing an election petition expired during the High Court’s notified vacation.

The vacation notification stated that the High Court would remain closed and provided only for vacation judges and officers to deal with urgent applications; it made no provision for filing election petitions.
The election petition was filed on the first day the High Court reopened.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the election petition was filed within time under Section 10 of the General Clauses Act and dismissed the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 81 and 86 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 prescribe the filing period for an election petition and provide for dismissal of a petition that does not comply with the statutory requirements. Sections 4 and 5 of the Limitation Act do not apply to election petitions, but Section 10 of the General Clauses Act applies where the court or office is closed on the last day of the prescribed period, allowing the act to be done on the next day it is open. The Court relied on Hukumdev Narain Yadav v. Lalit Narain Mishra, Hari Shanker Tripathi v. Shiv Harsh, and H.H. Raja Harinder Singh v. S. Karnail Singh.

rule.if: election_petition_case and limitation_expired_during_closure and ordinary_filing_facilities_closed and filed_on_first_reopening_day

predicates.election_petition_case: The proceeding concerns the filing deadline for an election petition.
predicates.limitation_expired_during_closure: The prescribed filing period ended while the court or its filing office was closed.
predicates.ordinary_filing_facilities_closed: The closure notice provided for limited urgent work but did not provide for ordinary filing of election petitions.
predicates.filed_on_first_reopening_day: The election petition was presented on the first day the court or filing office reopened.

issues.definition: If an election petition’s filing period ends during a closure that prevents ordinary filing and the petition is presented on the first reopening day, the filing is timely.
